title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Money, Dust, and the Thames

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, unhurried look at Charles Dickens's last completed novel.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel about money — where it comes from, what it does to people, and whether anyone survives it with their soul intact.
It opens with a body dragged from the Thames and ends with something very close to resurrection.
To help me unpack it, I have three guests whose company I suspect you will enjoy enormously.
Oliver Trevelyan has lent his voice to more classic novels on audio than almost anyone alive.
He approaches fiction as a performer first — which means he hears things the rest of us miss.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who specialises in exactly the kind of institutions Dickens spent his career anatomising.
He brings the real world in — the law, the workhouse, the money markets — and he is not always polite about what he finds.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite left it.
She will tell us what it feels like to live inside this book — what moves, what delights, what demands to be read aloud.
Welcome, all three of you.
Delighted to be here — and this is a novel I have lived inside for a very long time.
There is a sentence near the opening that I think announces the whole book's ambition in a single breath.
It is a novel about dust heaps — literal mountains of Victorian rubbish — and somehow Dickens makes them shimmer with meaning.
The Thames, the dust, the money — they are all the same thing in this book.
Filth and fortune are practically synonyms.
What strikes me first, coming back to this novel, is how precisely Dickens maps the anxiety of inherited wealth.
John Harmon returns from abroad to claim a fortune, and Dickens gives us his interior monologue in a passage that is almost forensic in its self-examination.
Harmon interrogates himself — quite literally — in the second person.
He says, in that strange, fractured soliloquy:
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
That repetition of 'shrinking' — twice — is not a slip.
It is the sound of a man physically recoiling from what he is about to become.
And notice Dickens gives him the instruction — 'Now, stop, and so far think it out, John Harmon' — as though the character must interrogate himself like a witness.
What I find so affecting in that passage is how lonely it is.
Harmon has no one to confess to — so he confesses to himself.
And money, in this novel, is almost always accompanied by that kind of isolation.
The people who have it — or are about to have it — cannot trust anyone around them.
And the people who are chasing it are even worse.
The chasing is where Dickens is at his most brilliantly vicious, I think.
There is a scene between Fledgeby and Lammle — two thoroughly unpleasant men conducting a thoroughly unpleasant negotiation — and it has a line that I find absolutely irresistible.
Fledgeby — who is described, with perfect economy, as having eyes too near together — is laying down terms.
And he says, with magnificent indignation:
'Don't you on that account come talking to me as if I was your doll and puppet, because I am not.'
A man with the meanest of eyes, defending his dignity.
It is comic, it is pathetic, and it is completely human — all at once.
That line works because Fledgeby is right, in a way — he really is being managed.
The Lammles are social predators of a very specific Victorian type — people who perform class to extract money from those who actually have it.
Fledgeby is graceless, but he sees clearly.
Dickens is quite interested in that combination — bad character paired with accurate perception.
And then there is the other end of the social spectrum — the Milveys, who are genuinely good and therefore constantly put upon.
There is a wonderful passage where they are trying to leave the house and are ambushed by their most exasperating parishioner, Mrs Sprodgkin.
Dickens describes her as possessing a sixth sense for knowing precisely when the Reverend Milvey least desired her company.
They buy her off with tea and bread and butter — and she accepts the gifts, but remains in the hall.
And then Dickens produces this extraordinary sentence:
'She regarded tea and sugar in the light of myrrh and frankincense, and considered bread and butter identical with locusts and wild honey.'
I have to laugh every time.
It is perfectly calibrated — the biblical register inflating the mundane to the sacred.
And the comic timing is entirely in the syntax — you cannot rush that sentence.
'Locusts and wild honey' — it lands like a punchline written by someone who understands that absurdity requires absolute deadpan.
Dickens is writing for the voice here — I am quite certain of it.
Money, manipulation, and a woman who will not leave the hall — we are firmly inside this novel's world already.
In the next segment, we are going to look more closely at the Thames itself — the river as setting, symbol, and source of the story's most unsettling energies.

segments.title: Bella's Reckoning: Gold Fever and Self-Discovery

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart sentence by sentence — and puts it back together again.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside one of the novel's most intricate storylines — the education of Bella Wilfer, and the moral drama playing out around her.
With me today are three extraordinary readers of this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels in audio than almost anyone alive — he hears Dickens the way a musician hears a score.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what it meant, in the 1860s, to be poor, to be female, and to be bequeathed to a stranger.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a critic who has re-read this novel more times than she's willing to admit — and who cares about Bella Wilfer with a fierceness that is frankly contagious.
Today's segment asks a central question: what does it take for Bella to see clearly — and what forces, human and financial, are conspiring to cloud that vision?
I want to start, if I may, with the architecture of John Harmon's confession — because it's one of the great narrative feats of the novel.
He's lying in a public-house bed, having nearly been murdered, and he decides — in that precarious recovery — to stage his own disappearance.
Dickens gives us the exact moment of the decision in this extraordinary sentence.
"the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella"
Proving Bella — as if she were a theorem to be demonstrated, or a coin to be tested for its true alloy.
The whole machinery of the plot hangs on those two words.
And it's worth pausing on exactly what Harmon is afraid of when he uses the phrase "perpetuating the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches."
In law, in this period, a testator could bind his heirs to conditions — including matrimonial ones — and those conditions ran with the money.
Old Harmon's will is a legal instrument of coercion masquerading as inheritance.
Young John's fear isn't sentimental — it's structural.
He has seen how money corrodes, and the scheme he hatches to dress as a common sailor and observe Bella directly is, in a way, his attempt to get outside the legal frame entirely.
Dickens is very precise about how that scheme formed — a shipboard confidence, a shared history, a plan to move in Bella's neighbourhood in disguise.
"the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way"
The gentry going native, you might say — if only briefly, and for entirely self-interested reasons.
What strikes me every time I read that confession is the phrase "moral timidity that dates from my childhood."
Harmon isn't just cautious — he's been damaged.
And yet the plan he devises — this surveillance of the woman he's supposed to marry — is troubling, isn't it?
He gets to observe Bella without her knowledge, to judge her, to form conclusions she has no power to contest.
And yet Dickens makes us want him to find her worthy.
That tension between sympathy and discomfort is exactly where the novel lives.
But I want to bring in the Boffin scenes, because that's where the real theatre happens.
There is a moment when Bella steals a glance at Boffin — just a look from under her eyelashes — and Dickens delivers this extraordinary image.
"A dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit, overshadowing the once open face."
Three nouns, one phrase — and a face disappears.
That is Dickens working at his absolute sharpest.
And then Boffin delivers what I can only call his sermon on the gospel of money.
It's worth hearing the whole of it — because it's both comic and genuinely sinister.
"Go in for money, my love. Money's the article. You'll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you'll live and die rich."
And then he savours the word — "R—r—rich!" — stretching it out like a man tasting something too sweet.
In the real world of the 1860s, this is not a parody — this is advice that respectable people actually gave to young women with good looks and no capital.
Dickens makes it grotesque, but he doesn't make it false.
And Bella has to sit there and receive that advice — from a man who was, until recently, the warmest, most guileless figure in her life.
That's what makes it so devastating.
It's not a stranger preaching greed at her — it's someone she trusted.
And then there's that passage with Rokesmith watching from the doorway — which I find almost unbearable to read.
Dickens holds the Secretary at a distance — watching, not touching, not speaking.

"The Secretary looked on from a doorway at the boofer lady thus encircled, and still looked on at the boofer lady standing alone there, when the determined old figure with its steady bright eyes was trudging through the streets, away from paralysis and pauperism."
Two people in the same frame — the old woman walking toward death with dignity, and the young woman being watched by the man who loves her.
Dickens compresses the whole novel into one doorway.
The word "boofer" does a remarkable amount of work in that sentence.
It's Johnny's word — a child's word for beautiful — and Rokesmith uses it in his private thoughts.
Which tells you everything about the quality of his feeling for her.
It's tender without being sentimental — which is the hardest thing in fiction to pull off.
I want to circle back to the charity passages, because they tell us something important about the world Bella is navigating.
Boffin's tirade about patrons and patronesses is, on the surface, pure comic ranting — but the target is real.
Victorian philanthropic culture was saturated with exactly this kind of title inflation — a mechanism for converting money into social prestige.
Listen to how Dickens piles up the categories.

"Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!"
The absurdity accumulates with each compound title until the whole edifice collapses under its own pomposity.
And Rokesmith sits at the centre of it — up to his neck — which is Boffin's very precise image for a man being drowned by other people's vanity.
And Bella is watching all of this — Boffin's transformation, Rokesmith's quiet suffering, the whole machinery of money and pretension grinding away around her.
She came into this household already infected by gold fever — she said so herself, quite openly, earlier in the novel.
And now she's being shown what gold fever actually looks like in a human face — that dark cloud of suspicion and covetousness.
The novel is using Boffin as a kind of terrible mirror.
A mirror she can't look away from — because she's living in his house, eating at his table.
And there is something almost pedagogical about the way the novel arranges things.
Bella is being educated — not in a schoolroom, but by a series of shocks to her moral imagination.
Boffin's unctuous "R—r—rich!" is one of those shocks.
It sounds like relish — but it curdles.
So we have John Harmon designing a test, Boffin delivering a gospel, and Rokesmith watching from a doorway — all circling the same question: what will Bella become?
And Dickens, in his supreme cunning, makes sure she has to earn her answer — that it can't be given to her, only discovered.
Coming up, we'll be turning to the river — and to the figures, living and dead, who haunt it.

segments.title: The Dust Heaps: Boffin's Moral Maze

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today we're deep inside one of the novel's great comic-and-moral engines: the Dust Heaps and the fortune they've created for Nicodemus Boffin.
The Golden Dustman has come into extraordinary wealth, and Dickens uses that fact to run a kind of controlled experiment in human nature.
What happens to people around money? What happens to the man holding it?
Oliver Trevelyan has spent more time inside Dickens's prose rhythms than perhaps anyone alive — he hears the performance written into the sentences.
James Blackstone brings the institutional and legal history — the real machinery behind the satire.
And Caroline Woodcourt has lived with this novel since she was a teenager and notices things the rest of us miss on a first reading.
Let's begin with the sheer spectacle of what arrives in Boffin's morning post.
The passage about the charitable letters is one of the great comic set-pieces in the whole novel, and I don't think it gets quite the attention it deserves.
Dickens is running through these categories of supplicant like a ringmaster with a whip — fifty-seven churches, forty-two parsonage houses, seven-and-twenty organs.
The accumulation itself is the joke — the sheer industrious scale of charitable exploitation.
But then the Duke of Linseed arrives, and Dickens just opens the letter and reads it to us.
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
Six words before the letter even opens, and we have the whole man.
The fatness of the envelope is the fatness of the duke's self-regard.
And then — the postscript. "The Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas." Thoughtful in the postscript, Dickens says, entirely straight-faced.
That letter is not entirely invented, you know.
The practice of recruiting wealthy names as charity stewards — at a fee — was entirely standard in Victorian philanthropic circles.
The steward's name appeared on the printed list, conferring respectability on the institution, while the institution extracted a tidy sum in exchange.

What Dickens captures beautifully is the lithographed intimacy — the letter is "sealed with ducal coronet" and addressed to Nicodemus Boffin "in quite another hand," meaning someone else filled in the name.
The personal address is a fiction. The warmth is manufactured. The whole apparatus of aristocratic condescension is mechanised.
That is a sharper observation about Victorian charity than many historians have managed.
What strikes me every time I re-read this passage is that Dickens keeps saying "dust" — different kinds of dust, useless dust, offered in exchange for real gold.
He calls the whole flood of solicitations "dust for ocular use" — things to throw in your eyes to obscure the real transaction.
The metaphor never lets you forget where the money came from, and what these people are really doing with their appeals.
And then there is that devastating phrase about the charities being in difficulties yet lavish in print and paper.
They cannot feed anyone but they can afford the expensive articles of correspondence.
Then we move from the institutional beggars to the individual ones, and Dickens is almost tender in his cruelty here.
He gives us the daughters of generals — "long accustomed to every luxury of life, except spelling" — and that parenthetical is a knife in a velvet glove.
But my favourite is the line about what these scraps of paper actually are.
"They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
You cannot improve on that. You simply cannot.
The simile is so exact and so absurd that it takes a moment to realise it's also a little tragic.
That passage on the individual beggars is one of the places where the comedy and the social horror become genuinely difficult to separate.
Consider the beggars of "punctual business-habits" — those who will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one on Tuesday if no postal order arrives.
Dickens is laughing at the precision — the memorandum, the exact time — but he is also describing the desperation that produces such letters.
People in Victorian England did write such letters. Poverty was that structured and that formal.
The novel holds both truths at once — it is funny and it is damning — and Dickens never tells you which to feel.
The husbands and wives passage undoes me slightly every time.
Wives writing without their husbands' knowledge, husbands writing without their wives' — the secrecy running in both directions simultaneously.
It's comic in its symmetry, but underneath it is something genuinely sad about what poverty does to trust between people.
And Dickens gets it all into a single subordinate clause, practically.
So Boffin is besieged from all sides — the great institutions, the aristocratic letter-writers, the desperate individuals.
But how does Boffin himself sit inside this grand mansion the money has purchased?
Dickens prepares us with one of his grandly mock-epic openings — "the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour" — and then just cuts to: Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire.
The deflation is the entire point.
And then comes the aristocratic family cheese.
"Like an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites."
The cheese! The simile is perfectly insane and perfectly right.
A great aristocratic house, like a great aristocratic cheese: too much of it, alive with creatures feeding on it, and fundamentally rather unpleasant to be near.
What I find touching is what follows immediately: he is content because Mrs Boffin enjoyed herself completely, and Miss Bella was delighted.
The mansion doesn't fit him; it is a kind of Legacy Duty, he thinks — an ongoing cost attached to wealth.
But his wife is happy. That is enough. Boffin at this point is genuinely good.
And Dickens is asking you to hold that alongside all the parasites and the corrupting pressure of the money.
The "perpetual Legacy Duty" phrase is doing precise legal work, as well as comic work.
Legacy Duty was a real tax on inherited estates in Victorian England — a percentage taken by the Crown on what you received.
Boffin is reframing the parasites — the hangers-on, the solicitors, the whole swarm — as the price of admission to wealth.
Which is, as an economic observation, more accurate than most of his contemporaries would admit.
Now — there is a will, and there is Silas Wegg, and there is the question of what happens when a genuinely bad man gets hold of a secret about money.
James, the contents of that document — the will Wegg claims to have found.
The will that Wegg presents is remarkable in its studied contempt — it is a document that expresses personality as much as legal intention.
Wegg reads it aloud, and the syntax is almost gleeful in its dismissiveness.

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
"Quite enough for him" — as a bequest, that clause is an insult dressed as a provision.
Harmon Senior hated everyone, including apparently the state — but he hated his family most, and this will is his final word.
Wegg thinks this document gives him power. That is the trap the novel is setting.
Wegg reading that will aloud is a performance of extraordinary vanity — he is casting himself as the man in control, the one who holds the secret.
And Dickens has prepared us for this character with almost biological precision.
Later, we see Wegg unable to sleep without first prowling past Boffin's house to feel his own power over it.
"Power — unless it be the power of intellect or virtue — has ever the greatest attraction for the lowest natures."
That is Dickens at his most magisterial and his most cold.
Not angry — just diagnostic. Wegg is a type as much as a man.
The image that follows that sentence is what stays with me — Wegg "defying the unconscious house-front" with his power to strip the roof off like a house of cards.
The house is unconscious. It doesn't know. The Boffins inside have no idea this man is circling them.
And Wegg gets a pleasure from that ignorance — their vulnerability is his entertainment.
It makes him repulsive in a very particular way — not grand villainy, just a small man feeding on the helplessness of people better than himself.
And we have just spent several pages watching those same people besieged by beggars and dukes. The novel is relentless.
What Dickens is tracing, across all these passages, is the way that a sudden fortune becomes a kind of lightning rod.
It draws everything to it — legitimate need, cynical exploitation, aristocratic condescension, and the darkest kind of resentment.
Boffin is the test case. What Wegg represents is the failure mode — power without virtue, as the novel says precisely.
The Dust Heaps cast a very long shadow in this novel.
The Dust Heaps as moral maze — with Boffin at the centre, Wegg circling like a bird of prey, and Dickens running his experiment in what money does to everyone it touches.
Oliver, James, Caroline — thank you.
After the break, we turn to what happens next — and to whether Boffin's goodness can survive the pressure the novel is about to put on it.
Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been circling the novel's great central mystery — who is John Harmon, and what does his disguise cost him?
This segment goes to the heart of it: identity, deception, and the shadow a dead man casts over the living.
Oliver Trevelyan has been waiting to get into the Boffins' memory of the seven-year-old John Harmon.
Oliver, over to you.
Thank you — and this passage undoes me every single time.
Dickens hands it to Boffin to narrate, and that is a stroke of absolute genius.
Because Boffin speaks in this wonderful vernacular — warm, slightly ungainly — and yet the emotion he carries is immense.
Listen to how he sets the scene — and I want to read this properly, because it deserves it.
That word — scanty — used twice in two breaths.
The clothes are scanty. The box is scanty. The child is barely there.
And then Dickens gives Mrs Boffin that cry:
The repetition of "wide wide world" — that's pure theatre, but it's also pure grief.
What strikes me is how that memory lodges in Mrs Boffin's body, not just her mind.
She wakes at night in a fright — when it's cold, when the wind roars — calling out for the child.
And the phrase Dickens uses is devastating in its quietness.
She cannot stop seeing his face as he looked up at them — that look of agony.
And it's that memory which drives her to want to adopt another orphan and name him John.
Which is itself extraordinary — she wants to give the name back to a living child.
And Mrs Boffin's proposal is quietly radical within the social logic of the novel.
She says it plainly, and I want to get the exact words right here.
The money couldn't save the real John Harmon — he drowned before he could inherit.
So she proposes redirecting that fortune toward a living child, an orphan, as an act of moral restitution.
That impulse is what the old miser could never extinguish in the Boffins — their basic human decency.
And Dickens is explicit about why old Harmon left them the estate in the first place.
He hated their integrity because it exposed the limits of his own power.
That line is almost Shakespearean in its irony — the miser's one honest act is to reward the people he couldn't corrupt.
And he mistrusted all mankind, Dickens says, except those who bore no resemblance to himself.
Which is a beautiful, devastating parenthesis.
Now — by the time we reach the confrontation with Wegg, all of that inheritance of trust and loyalty comes roaring to the surface.
John Harmon — the man who spent the entire novel hiding — finally gets to be himself, and he is furious.
What Dickens gives him is not a speech — it's controlled violence.
He says — and this is wonderful —
He's already knocking Wegg's head against the wall — and he wishes he could do worse.
And the comedy of it — the sheer comic fury — doesn't diminish the moral seriousness at all.
Because what follows is Harmon explaining, with extraordinary precision, what the Dutch bottle contained and what it means.
This is the passage that untangles the whole plot — and Dickens writes it as a tirade, which is the only fitting form.
Harmon repeats the phrase "Dutch bottle" like a drumbeat — four times in quick succession.
And right at the centre of it is this:
His sister — already dead of a broken heart — named and dismissed in the same breath.
That parenthesis is one of the cruelest things in all of Dickens.
The legal dimension of the bottle is also worth dwelling on.
Boffin buries the will — the latest will — rather than destroy it, because he fears the law.
Harmon explains it directly: Boffin "was afraid to destroy it, lest to destroy such a document... might be an offence at law."
That is a very precise legal anxiety — and it's accurate.
Suppressing a testamentary document could constitute fraud or obstruction.
So Boffin buries it — neither destroying it nor allowing it to act.
Which is actually a rather elegant moral compromise — and Dickens knows it.
And it all comes back to that seven-year-old boy in the yard, doesn't it.
The Boffins have been protecting John Harmon — or the idea of him — since before the novel begins.
And his disguise — his shadow-life as Rokesmith — is finally, furiously resolved because of that original loyalty.
Dickens ties the emotional knot and the legal knot at exactly the same moment — which is what makes the plotting feel inevitable rather than contrived.
Identity built on memory, preserved by loyalty, and revealed through fury — Dickens at his most architecturally ambitious.
We'll be back after the break to look at how the novel handles money — not as abstraction, but as living, corrupting force.

segments.title: The Comic Grotesque: Dickens's Savage Wit

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've spent time with the novel's darker currents — the river, the dust, the weight of money and death.
But Dickens is also, fiercely and brilliantly, a comic writer.
And this segment belongs to Oliver Trevelyan, who has spent a career performing Dickens's grotesques and hearing the comic machinery tick.
Oliver, where do you want to start?
I want to start with five words that T.S. Eliot once borrowed for the title of a poem.
Five words that come from the mouth of an old woman describing her ward's singular gift.
Betty Higden is explaining to her visitors that Sloppy — dear, ungainly, devoted Sloppy — reads the newspaper to her.
And then she says, with all the pride of a grandmother showing off a prodigy:
"He do the Police in different voices."
That ungrammatical little sentence contains the whole soul of oral performance.
Sloppy gives each policeman a different voice — he is actor, newspaper, and community storyteller all at once.
And Dickens writes it in Betty's grammar, not corrected grammar — which is itself an act of profound respect.
What strikes me every time I read that passage is the word "beautiful."
Betty says Sloppy is a "beautiful reader of a newspaper."
"He do the Police in different voices" is the proof of that beauty.
For these people, reading aloud IS the art form.
It's not a substitute for proper literacy — it is a form of genius in its own right.
And those different voices would have included magistrates, court reporters, constables — the whole apparatus of public order.
For people who had no reliable access to law or justice, the police reports were both entertainment and instruction.
Sloppy performing the police is, if you think about it, the powerless community performing power back at itself.
Dickens understood that completely — even in a throwaway comic line.
Now — the comic in this novel doesn't stay safely in the warm and tender register.
Dickens also has this magnificent capacity for savage physical comedy.
Consider the fate of Silas Wegg — the poem-selling, one-legged schemer who has spent the entire novel blackmailing Mr Boffin.
When John Harmon finally has enough of him, Dickens dispenses with Wegg in a sentence of almost physical pleasure.
"He found himself gripped by the cravat; shaken until his teeth chattered; shoved back, staggering, into a corner of the room; and pinned there."
Those semicolons are the beats of a choreographed thrashing.
Dickens times each indignity like a comedian landing punches.
It's so satisfying — almost indecently so.
Wegg has been so oily, so persistent, so small in his villainy.
And the punishment is purely kinetic — teeth chattering, staggering, pinned.
No speech, no moral lecture — just physics applied to a scoundrel.
And yet the comic violence directed at Wegg is entirely without legal consequence.
Which is, of course, the novel's fantasy — that class power can be physically and immediately reversed.
Wegg would, in reality, have had grounds for assault.
Dickens cheerfully ignores this — and we are entirely with him.
There's one more piece I want to bring in — and it works differently from both of those.
It's Mrs Boffin, at the novel's resolution, explaining to Bella why John Harmon kept delaying the great reveal.
And Dickens gives her this glorious, repeated comic rhythm — a structure of deferral that keeps building and building.
She reports John saying:
"She is such a cheerful, glorious housewife that I can't afford to be rich yet. I must wait a little longer."
And she reports him saying that again. And again.
The repetition IS the joke — but it's also a love letter, accumulating tenderness with every iteration.
Only Dickens can make "I must wait a little longer" into something that makes you want to cry and laugh simultaneously.
Mrs Boffin's voice in that speech is doing so much work.
She ends with "God bless you my Beauty, and God bless us all" — which is pure pantomime benevolence.
But you believe every word of it.
That's the trick — Dickens pushes the sentiment to the edge of excess, and then the sincerity rescues it.
The Boffins are interesting in this light because their benevolence is not ironic.
In a novel full of people corrupted by money, they inherit a fortune and become — generous.
It's almost subversive as a plot choice.
The comedy in Mrs Boffin's speech is inseparable from that moral conviction — she is funny because she is good.
That balance — funny because good — might be the most Dickensian thing you can say.
Oliver, before we move on — you have one more passage, and it's a very different kind of comedy altogether.
Yes — and I hesitate to call it comedy at all, except that it has this deranged, nightmarish quality that tips into something almost absurd.
It's John Harmon's account of the night he was drugged, attacked, and left for dead.
The prose mimics the fractured consciousness of a poisoned man — short declarative clauses, each one disconnected.
"I was turned over by a foot. I was dragged by the neck into a corner. I heard men speak together. I was turned over by other feet."
That repeated passive construction — I was turned, I was dragged — strips Harmon of all agency.
He is a body being moved by forces he can barely perceive.
And then — this is the line that stops me every time:
"I heard a noise of blows, and thought it was a wood-cutter cutting down a tree."
A man is being murdered and his poisoned brain reaches for — a wood-cutter in a forest.
That is not comedy. But it has the logic of a nightmare, which is the logic of dark farce.
The dissociation is what makes it so disturbing.
Harmon sees a figure lying in his own clothes on a bed — and cannot connect that figure to himself.
He literally witnesses his own apparent death from outside his own body.
"I could not have said that my name was John Harmon" — that's the sentence that opens up the whole theme of lost identity in the novel.
Every subsequent disguise and assumed name flows from this moment of genuine self-erasure.
And legally, of course, John Harmon ceases to exist at that moment.
A man presumed drowned with his identity transferred to a corpse — the inheritance law of the period would have treated that as death in fact.
His subsequent existence as Rokesmith is, in strict legal terms, a ghost's existence.
The grotesque in this passage isn't comic at all — it is the machinery of the novel's entire plot made visceral.
From Sloppy doing the police in different voices, to Wegg's teeth chattering, to a man losing his name in a poisoned nightmare — Dickens's comic range is extraordinary.
Coming up, we'll look at the women of this novel — and what the book asks of them, and what it gives them in return.

segments.title: Society's Rotten Foundation: What Our Mutual Friend Reveals

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart — with love and considerable relish.
Our Mutual Friend is a book about money — who has it, who pretends to, who is destroyed by wanting it, and the very few who manage to stay human in its presence.
Today we're asking what this novel reveals about the rotten foundation beneath Victorian society's polished surface.
With me are three people I trust completely to do the book justice.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels than almost anyone alive, and he reads Dickens the way Dickens intended — for the ear, for the room, for the laugh and the sting.
Professor James Blackstone brings the legal and social history — he knows what these institutions actually were, and he is not sentimental about them.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens — she catches what makes you stop mid-sentence and read the thing again.
Let's begin with the Boffins — because if you want to understand what Dickens is doing in this novel, the Boffins are where you start.
The Boffins are Dickens's great test case in this novel.
They inherit sudden, enormous wealth from old Harmon — wealth built on dust heaps, on refuse, on the literal garbage of London.
And the question the novel poses immediately is: will that wealth corrupt them, or can decency survive it?
There's a passage early on — Mr Boffin has been reflecting on his wife's character, and he turns to her and says something quite simple.
'Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!'
And Dickens's response to that tenderness is absolutely devastating in its comic precision.
He writes that this was ruin to Mrs Boffin's social aspirations — and that they sat, quote, 'a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.'
The capital U on Unfashionable is doing extraordinary work — Dickens is making fashionability itself a named, contemptible institution.
That capital U stopped me the first time I read it as a teenager, and it still stops me.
Because what Dickens is saying is that genuine affection — this man's real love for his wife, expressed plainly — is the very thing that disqualifies them from polite society.
Fashionable society in this novel runs on performance and pretence.
The Veneerings, the Podsnaps — they are architecture built entirely of surfaces.
And then you get this lovely, hopeless pair sitting side by side, and somehow they are the moral centre of the whole novel.
The satire and the tenderness are completely inseparable — that's the particular genius of this book.
'A hopelessly Unfashionable pair' — I want that on a gravestone, frankly.
What James is identifying is something Dickens does throughout this novel: the satirical blow lands inside a moment of warmth.
You're charmed and indicted simultaneously.
But I want to talk about a different kind of Dickensian energy — the pure comic grotesque, which this novel does better than almost any other.
There's a scene involving an orphan — a very small, very round orphan — and his encounter with the street.
'Being an orphan of a chubby conformation, he then took to rolling, and had rolled into the gutter before they could come up.'
'A chubby conformation' — Dickens is essentially doing a physics lecture on why small round children roll.
And then the situation escalates magnificently — John Rokesmith rescues the child, and the first impression given to Mrs Higden is of two strangers holding an upside-down, purple infant.
It is funny, and I don't want to drain the comedy from it — but there is something underneath that scene worth naming.
Mrs Higden runs a minding establishment — she cares for children, including orphans, as a private arrangement, precisely because the alternative is the workhouse.
The workhouse looms over this entire novel as a kind of ultimate degradation — and the terror of it is entirely rational, given what the workhouse actually was.
So when this small round child rolls into the gutter and ends up purple and upside down in a stranger's arms — the laughter is real, but so is the precariousness underneath it.
Dickens never lets you have the comedy clean — there's always that catch in the throat.
That phrase 'a lugubrious and inhuman character' — applied to the cries of a child — is almost unbearably precise.
You laugh at 'lugubrious,' and then you sit with 'inhuman,' and they're the same moment.
And then on the other end of the moral spectrum from these vulnerable children — we have Silas Wegg.
Wegg is one of Dickens's supreme comic villains — venal, self-important, magnificently deluded about his own importance.
There's a scene where Wegg and his associate Mr Venus are reading through documents and discover something they believe to be financially significant.
'Both remaining in a kind of pecuniary swoon.'
'A pecuniary swoon' — I have read those three words aloud more times than I can count, and they never fail.
Because it's physically exact — Wegg has actually toppled sideways, his wooden leg elevated, squeezing poor Venus against the settle — and it's also morally exact.
Greed, in this novel, is a kind of fainting fit — a loss of consciousness, a loss of self.
Wegg is also a figure of class resentment rendered grotesque — he is lower-middle-class, self-educated, deeply aggrieved by his own marginal status.
And he attaches himself to the Boffins precisely because their sudden elevation strikes him as fundamentally illegitimate — people like the Boffins aren't supposed to have money.
The novel uses Wegg to expose a particular Victorian pathology: the conviction that inherited status, however threadbare, outranks earned or acquired wealth.
And yet Wegg never achieves genuine menace — Dickens won't allow it — because he is finally too absurd.
There's a moment late in the novel where Wegg is at the keyhole of Boffin's room, and his chosen form of intimidation is — miming a grindstone.
'Silas made no reply, but laboured with a will at turning an imaginary grindstone outside the keyhole, while Mr Boffin stooped at it within; he then laughed silently, and stumped home.'
'Laughed silently, and stumped home' — I want to perform that sentence every day of my life.
The wooden leg stumping home after a silent evil laugh — it is pantomime villain written at the level of genius.
What strikes me about that passage is the word 'imaginary' — the grindstone is imaginary, but the power dynamic is real enough to make Boffin stoop.
There's something genuinely unsettling in there, amid all the grotesque comedy.
The Boffins — that hopelessly Unfashionable pair — are being ground down by someone whose only weapon is performance and pretence.
Which brings us back to what James said at the start: fashionable society and Silas Wegg are, at root, doing exactly the same thing.
That is a connection I'll be sitting with for some time.
Pretence as power — the grindstone and the dinner party operating on the same principle.
We'll continue in a moment — there's much more novel to unpick, and a great deal more Dickens has to say about what money does to people who suddenly find themselves holding it.

segments.title: Closing: Redemption in a World of Objects

utterances.text: We've spent this episode moving through a world preoccupied with money, dust, and the question of what a human being is actually worth.
So it seems right to close where the novel itself keeps returning — to the question of whether anyone in that world can actually change.
Bella Wilfer is Dickens's great test case for that question, and I want to bring in Caroline first, because I know she has strong feelings about what happens to Bella in these middle chapters.
Yes — and what I love is that Dickens doesn't make Bella's transformation a smooth or flattering process.
He makes her catch herself in the act of being exactly who she doesn't want to be.
There's a scene where Mr Boffin has said something perfectly sensible about money — sensible in the way Bella herself thinks — and she comes away from the conversation feeling vaguely soiled.
And she goes to her room and interrogates herself in the looking-glass.

'What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it. Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?'
That looking-glass is doing so much work in this novel — she keeps returning to it, and each time it's both vanity and conscience at once.
'You inconsistent little Beast' — said to oneself in the mirror — that is one of the great comic self-lacerations in English fiction.
The comedy and the moral seriousness are completely inseparable there.
And then it happens again — later, wonderfully — when Bella is with Lizzie Hexam and Lizzie says something about selfless love.
Bella's response is to give herself — and I love that Dickens spells this out — a penitential poke in the side.
'There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?'
The self-address, the physical punishment, the sheer indignity of it — and it's funny, and it's also entirely real.
What strikes me historically is how radical Bella's trajectory actually is, set against the economic reality of her position.
A young woman of Bella's class in the 1860s had almost no economic agency whatsoever — marriage was not a romantic preference, it was the mechanism of material survival.
When Bella calls herself mercenary and means it as a reproach, she is fighting against the entire logic of her society.
Dickens understands that — which is why the self-criticism is comic rather than simply moralistic.
The comedy gives her a way out of self-condemnation that a straightforward moral lecture never could.
And then Dickens gives us something that changes the register entirely — the scene where Lizzie speaks about Eugene.
It's one of the most quietly devastating passages in the book, I think.
Lizzie describes the first time Eugene's eyes looked at her — on a wretched night, by the river — and she says she hopes they never look at her again.
'I would not have the light of them taken out of my life, for anything my life can give me.'
She loves him, she knows it's impossible, she wants him gone — and yet that light is the thing she can't surrender.
That is not sentiment — that is precision.
And notice what Lizzie says immediately after — that she hadn't intended to tell any of this, not a single word, until the moment Bella walked in.
'You came in, and my mind changed.'
Four words — and they carry the whole weight of what human presence can do for another person.
This is the counter-weight to all the money and the dust and the market in everything — this thing that happens between two people in a room.
It's also the novel testing what genuine connection costs, which is a deeply practical question in Dickens's world.
Lizzie is working-class, isolated, endangered — her capacity to trust Bella with this is itself a form of courage the novel asks us to register.
And Bella receives it — takes the poke in the side, as Oliver says — and something shifts.
And I think that's exactly where this novel does something rather extraordinary — it earns its redemptions not through argument but through accumulated small moments of honesty.
A woman confronting herself in a looking-glass, a poke in the ribs, four words spoken in a room — these are the units of change in this world.
My warmest thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has done justice to one of Dickens's most capacious and surprising novels.
Our Mutual Friend — still unfolding, still worth every page.

But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.

‘Exactly so, sir!’ returned Wegg, blandly and buoyantly. ‘I see I take you
      with me! Hear, hear, hear! Resolved, as your discriminating good sense
      perceives, that if you was to have a sap—pur— ize , it should be
      a complete one! Well, sir. And so, as you have honoured me by
      anticipating, I examined the document. Regularly executed, regularly
      witnessed, very short. Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever
      had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the
      Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and
      residue of his property to the Crown.’
c40:p31.summary: Wegg describes the will's contents: John Harmon leaves the Little Mound to Boffin and the remainder to the Crown, having no close relationships.
c40:p31.best_quote: Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown.

c40:p97.text:
For, Silas Wegg felt it to be quite out of the question that he could lay
      his head upon his pillow in peace, without first hovering over Mr Boffin’s
      house in the superior character of its Evil Genius. Power (unless it be
      the power of intellect or virtue) has ever the greatest attraction for the
      lowest natures; and the mere defiance of the unconscious house-front, with
      his power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a
      house of cards, was a treat which had a charm for Silas Wegg.
c40:p97.summary: Wegg cannot rest without hovering over Boffin's house, fantasizing about his power to destroy it, demonstrating how power appeals to base natures.
c40:p97.best_quote: Power (unless it be the power of intellect or virtue) has ever the greatest attraction for the lowest natures; and the mere defiance of the unconscious house-front, with his power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a house of cards, was a treat which had a charm for Silas Wegg.

c8:p43.text:
‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’
c8:p43.summary: Boffin recounts the last time he and Mrs Boffin saw young John Harmon, a seven-year-old being sent to a foreign school, including the poignant moment when Mrs Boffin wept while warming the boy by the fire and embraced him protectively, expressing a desire to save him—a memory that haunted her for years.
c8:p43.best_quote: There was his little scanty travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the steamboat... Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come into the child's eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, "I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!"

c9:p23.text:
Mrs Boffin pulled his nearest ear, in acknowledgment of this piece of
      philosophy, and then said, gradually toning down to a motherly strain:
      ‘Last, and not least, I have taken a fancy. You remember dear little John
      Harmon, before he went to school? Over yonder across the yard, at our
      fire? Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it’s come to us, I
      should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and
      give him John’s name, and provide for him. Somehow, it would make me
      easier, I fancy. Say it’s only a whim—’
c9:p23.summary: Mrs Boffin proposes adopting an orphan child, naming him John Harmon in memory of the young heir who drowned, thereby using their inherited fortune for redemptive good.
c9:p23.best_quote: Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him.

c9:p30.text:
Through his most inveterate purposes, the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail had
      known these two faithful servants to be honest and true. While he raged at
      them and reviled them for opposing him with the speech of the honest and
      true, it had scratched his stony heart, and he had perceived the
      powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to
      the attempt. So, even while he was their griping taskmaster and never gave
      them a good word, he had written their names down in his will. So, even
      while it was his daily declaration that he mistrusted all mankind—and
      sorely indeed he did mistrust all who bore any resemblance to himself—he
      was as certain that these two people, surviving him, would be trustworthy
      in all things from the greatest to the least, as he was that he must
      surely die.
c9:p30.summary: Dickens explains that old John Harmon, despite his misanthropy and greed, respected the Boffins' moral integrity so deeply that he named them in his will as trustees of his fortune.
c9:p30.best_quote: he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt

c64:p95.text:
‘I mean to knock your head against the wall,’ returned John Harmon,
      suiting his action to his words, with the heartiest good will; ‘and I’d
      give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out. Listen, you
      scoundrel, and look at that Dutch bottle.’
c64:p95.summary: Harmon violently interrogates Wegg while ordering Sloppy to hold up the Dutch bottle, explaining its significance and his own indebtedness to Boffin.
c64:p95.best_quote: and I'd give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out.

c64:p97.text:
‘That Dutch bottle, scoundrel, contained the latest will of the many wills
      made by my unhappy self-tormenting father. That will gives everything
      absolutely to my noble benefactor and yours, Mr Boffin, excluding and
      reviling me, and my sister (then already dead of a broken heart), by name.
      That Dutch bottle was found by my noble benefactor and yours, after he
      entered on possession of the estate. That Dutch bottle distressed him
      beyond measure, because, though I and my sister were both no more, it cast
      a slur upon our memory which he knew we had done nothing in our miserable
      youth, to deserve. That Dutch bottle, therefore, he buried in the Mound
      belonging to him, and there it lay while you, you thankless wretch, were
      prodding and poking—often very near it, I dare say. His intention
      was, that it should never see the light; but he was afraid to destroy it,
      lest to destroy such a document, even with his great generous motive,
      might be an offence at law. After the discovery was made here who I was,
      Mr Boffin, still restless on the subject, told me, upon certain conditions
      impossible for such a hound as you to appreciate, the secret of that Dutch
      bottle. I urged upon him the necessity of its being dug up, and the paper
      being legally produced and established. The first thing you saw him do,
      and the second thing has been done without your knowledge. Consequently,
      the paper now rattling in your hand as I shake you—and I should like
      to shake the life out of you—is worth less than the rotten cork of
      the Dutch bottle, do you understand?’
c64:p97.summary: Harmon explains how the Dutch bottle was found by Boffin after entering the estate, buried in the Mound to hide its contents, and later exhumed without Wegg's knowledge.
c64:p97.best_quote: That Dutch bottle, scoundrel, contained the latest will of the many wills made by my unhappy self-tormenting father. That will gives everything absolutely to my noble benefactor and yours, Mr Boffin, excluding and reviling me, and my sister (then already dead of a broken heart), by name.

c16:p31.text:
‘For I aint, you must know,’ said Betty, ‘much of a hand at reading
      writing-hand, though I can read my Bible and most print. And I do love a
      newspaper. You mightn’t think it, but Sloppy is a beautiful reader of a
      newspaper. He do the Police in different voices.’
c16:p31.summary: Betty Higden explains that Sloppy reads aloud to her beautifully, particularly the newspapers in different voices, compensating for her own limited literacy.
c16:p31.best_quote: He do the Police in different voices.

c64:p92.text:
Wegg had repeated the word with a sneer, and was entering on some
      sarcastic retort, when, to his boundless amazement, he found himself
      gripped by the cravat; shaken until his teeth chattered; shoved back,
      staggering, into a corner of the room; and pinned there.
c64:p92.summary: Harmon physically grabs Wegg by the cravat and shakes him violently, throwing him into a corner of the room.

c63:p42.text:
‘And so, my good and pretty,’ pursued Mrs Boffin, ‘you was married, and
      there was we hid up in the church-organ by this husband of yours; for he
      wouldn’t let us out with it then, as was first meant. “No,” he says,
      “she’s so unselfish and contented, that I can’t afford to be rich yet. I
      must wait a little longer.” Then, when baby was expected, he says, “She is
      such a cheerful, glorious housewife that I can’t afford to be rich yet. I
      must wait a little longer.” Then when baby was born, he says, “She is so
      much better than she ever was, that I can’t afford to be rich yet. I must
      wait a little longer.” And so he goes on and on, till I says outright,
      “Now, John, if you don’t fix a time for setting her up in her own house
      and home, and letting us walk out of it, I’ll turn Informer.” Then he says
      he’ll only wait to triumph beyond what we ever thought possible, and to
      show her to us better than even we ever supposed; and he says, “She shall
      see me under suspicion of having murdered myself, and  you  shall see how
      trusting and how true she’ll be.” Well! Noddy and me agreed to that, and
      he was right, and here you are, and the horses is in, and the story is
      done, and God bless you my Beauty, and God bless us all!’
c63:p42.summary: Mrs Boffin completes the narrative: John repeatedly postponed revealing himself because Bella kept improving; only after much urging does he agree to test her by allowing her to witness suspicion of his involvement in his own murder.
c63:p42.best_quote: She is such a cheerful, glorious housewife that I can't afford to be rich yet. I must wait a little longer.

c30:p17.text:
‘I had drank some coffee, when to my sense of sight he began to swell
      immensely, and something urged me to rush at him. We had a struggle near
      the door. He got from me, through my not knowing where to strike, in the
      whirling round of the room, and the flashing of flames of fire between us.
      I dropped down. Lying helpless on the ground, I was turned over by a foot.
      I was dragged by the neck into a corner. I heard men speak together. I was
      turned over by other feet. I saw a figure like myself lying dressed in my
      clothes on a bed. What might have been, for anything I knew, a silence of
      days, weeks, months, years, was broken by a violent wrestling of men all
      over the room. The figure like myself was assailed, and my valise was in
      its hand. I was trodden upon and fallen over. I heard a noise of blows,
      and thought it was a wood-cutter cutting down a tree. I could not have
      said that my name was John Harmon—I could not have thought it—I
      didn’t know it—but when I heard the blows, I thought of the
      wood-cutter and his axe, and had some dead idea that I was lying in a
      forest.
c30:p17.summary: John Harmon recounts his drugged attack, struggling with Radfoot, losing consciousness, seeing another figure dressed in his clothes, and experiencing violent confusion before apparently drowning.
c30:p17.best_quote: I saw a figure like myself lying dressed in my clothes on a bed. What might have been, for anything I knew, a silence of days, weeks, months, years, was broken by a violent wrestling of men all over the room.

c9:p28.text:
‘Yes; and it’s pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin,’ said her
      husband, ‘and it’s been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a
      year!’ It was ruin to Mrs Boffin’s aspirations, but, having so spoken,
      they sat side by side, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.
c9:p28.summary: Mr Boffin lovingly affirms his wife's moral character, but Dickens narrates that their virtuous intentions doom their social aspirations to fashionability.
c9:p28.best_quote: Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!

c16:p25.text:
It unfortunately happened as they quickened their pace, that the orphan,
      lost to considerations of personal safety in the ardour of the moment,
      overbalanced himself and toppled into the street. Being an orphan of a
      chubby conformation, he then took to rolling, and had rolled into the
      gutter before they could come up. From the gutter he was rescued by John
      Rokesmith, and thus the first meeting with Mrs Higden was inaugurated by
      the awkward circumstance of their being in possession—one would say
      at first sight unlawful possession—of the orphan, upside down and
      purple in the countenance. The board across the doorway too, acting as a
      trap equally for the feet of Mrs Higden coming out, and the feet of Mrs
      Boffin and John Rokesmith going in, greatly increased the difficulty of
      the situation: to which the cries of the orphan imparted a lugubrious and
      inhuman character.
c16:p25.summary: The orphan tumbles from the doorway board and rolls into the gutter, where John Rokesmith rescues him just as he and Mrs Boffin arrive, creating an awkward first encounter with Mrs Higden.
c16:p25.best_quote: Being an orphan of a chubby conformation, he then took to rolling, and had rolled into the gutter before they could come up.

c39:p83.text:
On the way to this crisis Mr Wegg’s wooden leg had gradually elevated
      itself more and more, and he had nudged Mr Venus with his opposite elbow
      deeper and deeper, until at length the preservation of his balance became
      incompatible with the two actions, and he now dropped over sideways upon
      that gentleman, squeezing him against the settle’s edge. Nor did either of
      the two, for some few seconds, make any effort to recover himself; both
      remaining in a kind of pecuniary swoon.
c39:p83.summary: Wegg's escalating excitement during the reading causes him to lose balance and collapse against Venus, both falling into a state of rapture over the revelations of hidden wealth.
c39:p83.best_quote: both remaining in a kind of pecuniary swoon.

c53:p125.text:
This time Silas made no reply, but laboured with a will at turning an
      imaginary grindstone outside the keyhole, while Mr Boffin stooped at it
      within; he then laughed silently, and stumped home.
c53:p125.summary: Wegg silently mines turning a grindstone at the keyhole while Boffin watches helplessly from within; Wegg then laughs and departs.
c53:p125.best_quote: This time Silas made no reply, but laboured with a will at turning an imaginary grindstone outside the keyhole, while Mr Boffin stooped at it within; he then laughed silently, and stumped home.

c38:p55.text:
Somehow, Bella was not so well pleased with this assurance and this
      prospect as she might have been. Somehow, when she put her arms round Mrs
      Boffin’s neck and said Good Night, she derived a sense of unworthiness
      from the still anxious face of that good woman and her obvious wish to
      excuse her husband. ‘Why, what need to excuse him?’ thought Bella, sitting
      down in her own room. ‘What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very
      true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don’t I like it
      then? No, I don’t like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I
      disparage him for it. Then pray,’ said Bella, sternly putting the question
      to herself in the looking-glass as usual, ‘what do you mean by this, you
      inconsistent little Beast?’
c38:p55.summary: Alone in her room, Bella grapples with her confused reaction to Mr Boffin's advice: she finds his sentiments sensible and true to her own desires, yet she is repelled by them and finds herself disparaging him for expressing them, finally questioning herself severely in the mirror.
c38:p55.best_quote: Why, what need to excuse him? What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it. Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?

c42:p156.text:
The question was so directly at variance with Bella’s views in life, as
      set forth to her father, that she said internally, ‘There, you little
      mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain’t you ashamed of your self?’ and
      unclasped the girdle of her arms, expressly to give herself a penitential
      poke in the side.
c42:p156.summary: Bella experiences an internal moment of shame at her own mercenary values when confronted by Lizzie's selfless love, and literally punishes herself with a poke in the side.
c42:p156.best_quote: There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?

c42:p162.text:
‘It was late upon a wretched night,’ said Lizzie, ‘when his eyes first
      looked at me in my old river-side home, very different from this. His eyes
      may never look at me again. I would rather that they never did; I hope
      that they never may. But I would not have the light of them taken out of
      my life, for anything my life can give me. I have told you everything now,
      my dear. If it comes a little strange to me to have parted with it, I am
      not sorry. I had no thought of ever parting with a single word of it, a
      moment before you came in; but you came in, and my mind changed.’
c42:p162.summary: Lizzie recalls the rainy night she first met Eugene and confesses that sharing her feelings with Bella has been healing, though unexpected.
c42:p162.best_quote: I would not have the light of them taken out of my life, for anything my life can give me.
